newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Port captures Albania's bleak chaos.
newsitem.headline: Port captures Albania's bleak chaos.

text.p: Albania's largest port is a place so devoid of life even the seagulls have flown away.

The harbour at Durres is empty, its warehouses looted and fire-scorched. Giant cargo cranes stand silent, silhouetted against the sky with massive chains dangling from their gantries like hangman's nooses.
Rusted steel machine parts, spawling concrete and smouldering piles of rubbish line the quay.

No ship, not even a fishing boat, dares dock without an armed guard for fear of being swamped by the thousands of Albanians who have gathered on the port's perimeter hoping to gain passage out of the country as refugees.

Daily skirmishes between would-be refugees and local police provide the only speck of colour in a city whose dusty, faded green and yellow facades attest to the widespread poverty in Europe's poorest country.
Residents crane their necks skyward at the sound of helicopters beating through the air high over the city.
American, French, German and Italian military units are ferrying foreign nationals out of the country from staging points in the capital Tirana and on beaches south of Durres.
"I wish that Greece would invade us so we could surrender to them and this would all be over," confides Mirella, a 25-year old Albanian hoping to leave Durres on a boat.
"Albania is finished. There's nothing more for us here. The government and the mafia have stolen everything. I completed school, I speak English, but I have no job."
Mirella is lucky because she has friends with whom to stay in Durres while keeping an eye on the harbour for any sign of a ship entering.
Thousands of Albanians gathered here from outside the city are living rough. Sunburned, filthy, redolent of stale sweat and smoke from campfires, they are mostly young males.
When pyramid investment schemes recently collapsed in Albania so did public order, especially in the south, where there was a spasm of looting and police and army forces were driven out.
Local citizens' committees have been formed in the south but real power in that region rests with clan-based mafia groups who were active even before the troubles.
Durres pulled back from the brink late last week and remains firmly under government control. The worst day here was Thursday when looting and arson erupted in parts of the city.
A Italianate villa built by Albania's King before World War Two, and used more recently by President Sali Berisha, was thoroughly trashed by hooligans.

All of the villa's furniture and kitchen and bathroom fixtures have been carted away. Doors are shattered or ripped from their frames and all the windows are broken. A central marble staircase has been largely destroyed.
On Sunday children were romping through the debris throwing huge chunks of marble out windows and off balconies. Old women were digging up the best shrubs from the garden.

Albania is chaotic, more so in the south than elsewhere, but person-on-person violence is still relatively rare despite the fact that many armouries have been looted. There is no ethnic or religious tinge to the country's discontent.
Although many people blame President Berisha for the pyramid scandal they seem to have given up all realistic expectation of ever getting their money back.
The real enemy in Albania now is boredom and anxiety. After a while even young men grow tired of standing by the side of the road and firing their Kalashnikovs into the air for lack of a target.
